title: Plugin CI, hooks and managed settings

story: On a Thursday, a frontend lead fixes a wrong command in the verify skill, the skill people and agents use before they say a change is done. The pull request is two lines, it is approved and merged, and a week later stable is promoted. Three weeks after that, someone notices that Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, still runs the old command. So does every laptop. The lead forgot to raise the plugin's version, so no machine ever replaced its copy, and nothing anywhere showed an error.

The same week, another pull request adds a small Python file under hooks/ and one line to hooks.json. The reviewer reads it the way they read a skill, as text, and approves. From then on that script runs before every file edit, on every laptop and on every agent machine that has the plugin.
hook.question: A plugin change reaches every machine and some of it runs as code. What should be checked automatically before it merges, and what should the reviewer be told?

read.h: Claude Code forgives, so mistakes are silent
p: Claude Code is built to keep working when a plugin is slightly wrong. A field it does not know is ignored. A hook under an event name it does not know, such as PreToolUsee with one letter too many, is ignored too, so the guard you wrote never runs. A plugin whose version did not change keeps its cached copy, so a fix never arrives. None of these stops a session, and none shows an error to the person using it, which is good for that person and bad for whoever maintains the plugin.

Plugin CI is the place where these quiet failures become loud. Its first step runs claude plugin validate on the catalog and on every plugin. Without flags, validate reports problems as warnings and still passes. With --strict it treats every warning as an error and exits with code 1, so the pull request shows a red check instead of a hook that silently does nothing on every machine.

read.h: A changed plugin needs a higher version
p: The Thursday problem needs a check that validate cannot do, because validate looks at the files as they are and knows nothing about the branch they came from. The version check compares two commits: the base branch the pull request wants to merge into, and its head. For every plugin with a changed file under plugins/<name>/, the version in that plugin's plugin.json must be higher at the head than at the base. Otherwise the job fails and says which file to edit.
It is a small script in Python using only the standard library, like our hooks, so it runs anywhere git and python3 are installed.

code.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Fail when a plugin's files changed but its version in plugin.json did not go up."""
import json
import subprocess
import sys

base = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "origin/main"


def git(*args):
    return subprocess.run(["git", *args], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout


def version(ref, plugin):
    text = git("show", f"{ref}:plugins/{plugin}/.claude-plugin/plugin.json")
    return tuple(int(x) for x in json.loads(text)["version"].split(".")) if text else None


show = lambda v: ".".join(map(str, v))
changed = sorted({p.split("/")[1] for p in git("diff", "--name-only", f"{base}...HEAD").split() if p.startswith("plugins/")})
bad = 0
for plugin in changed:
    old, new = version(base, plugin), version("HEAD", plugin)
    if old is None:
        print(f"✔ {plugin}: new plugin at {show(new)}")
    elif new is None or new <= old:
        bad += 1
        print(f"✘ {plugin}: files changed but the version is still {show(old)}; raise it in plugins/{plugin}/.claude-plugin/plugin.json")
    else:
        print(f"✔ {plugin}: {show(old)} -> {show(new)}")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)

notes.text: The base branch, origin/main in CI, so the check sees exactly what the pull request changes.
git show <ref>:<path> reads a file as it was at that commit, without checking it out.
Versions become tuples of numbers, so 0.10.0 is higher than 0.9.0, which a plain string comparison would get wrong.
Only plugins with a changed file are checked. The three-dot diff compares the head with the point where the branch left the base.
A changed plugin whose version did not go up: the Thursday mistake.

read.see: ✘ rhino-core: files changed but the version is still 0.4.0; raise it in plugins/rhino-core/.claude-plugin/plugin.json

read.h: Some changes run code on every machine
p: Most of a plugin is text that Claude reads. A few parts are different, because they run without anyone reading them. A hook is a command Claude Code starts on every matching event. An MCP server in .mcp.json is a program that starts with the session. Files in bin/ or scripts/ are executables the plugin calls. And allowed-tools in a skill's frontmatter lets the listed tools run without a permission prompt while that skill is active. A change to any of these runs on every laptop and every agent machine that has the plugin, so it deserves to be read as code.

The risk job finds these changes with two git diff commands: one over the changed file paths, one over SKILL.md lines that add or remove allowed-tools. When it finds something, it adds a high-risk label to the pull request and posts one comment that lists the files, edited in place on later pushes so it does not repeat. The label does not add an approver. The repository still needs exactly one approval; the label tells that one reviewer to run the plugin on their own machine before approving. A second job scans the pull request's commits for secrets with gitleaks, a scanner that finds keys and tokens in git history.

code.text:
base=origin/main
git diff --name-only "$base"...HEAD | grep -E '(^|/)(hooks|bin|scripts|monitors)/|\.mcp\.json$'
git diff "$base"...HEAD -- '**/SKILL.md' | grep -E '^[+-](allowed-tools|disallowed-tools):'

notes.text: Paths whose files run as programs, plus MCP server configuration.
Added or removed lines in skill frontmatter that change which tools run without asking.

read.h: Required, pinned, and only then the evals
p: A check that can be skipped protects nothing, so plugin-ci / validate is a required check in the repository's ruleset: GitHub refuses the merge until it is green. The workflow installs one exact version of Claude Code, because a newer validator can add warnings, and with --strict a new warning would turn every open pull request red on the same morning. Renovate, our dependency-update bot, raises that version through a pull request of its own.

These checks are cheap and need no model. Only after they pass does the evals job run each changed plugin's eval cases with and without the plugin, the gate from the evals lesson, because a skill can be perfectly valid and still make results worse.

deeper.h: Go deeper: from merge to every laptop with managed settings
p: Once a change has passed CI, been promoted to stable and raised its version, managed settings, the company-wide settings layer that nobody can override on their own laptop, decide which machines load it. Our policy registers the rhino marketplace at stable, turns rhino-core on for everyone, allows marketplaces only from our own GitHub organization (plus Anthropic's official one), and allows MCP servers only by URL from a reviewed list. The rollout starts with an inventory of what people already use, because an MCP allow-list also blocks claude.ai connectors such as Jira or Slack.

An allow-list entry for a GitHub marketplace must match its ref exactly: an entry without a ref does not cover a marketplace added at #stable. So the policy lists the stable ref explicitly. Agent machines get the same policy file and a seed folder with the stable plugins already in it (the image is built with them), so Nova runs what people run without cloning anything at start.

lab.title: Make the quiet failures loud
lab.goal: Build a small plugin repository, then write and run the checks that catch a missing version bump, a hook that would be ignored, and a change that runs code on every machine.

guess.q: A pull request changes one line of the verify skill and leaves rhino-core at 0.4.0. claude plugin validate --strict runs on it. What does validate say?

options.text: It fails, because the content changed but the version did not
options.why: validate looks only at the files as they are now. It cannot know what the base branch had.

options.text: It passes. Catching the missing bump needs a script that compares the base branch with the head
options.why: That is why plugin CI has a separate version check next to validate.

options.text: It passes with a warning that the version looks old
options.why: No version number looks old to validate; 0.4.0 is a fine version on its own.

lab.build: validate does not check that a skill's name field matches its folder, and a mismatch breaks every reference to the skill. Write scripts/check_skills.py: for every plugins/*/skills/*/SKILL.md, read the frontmatter between the first two --- lines, and fail when name differs from the folder name, or when description plus when_to_use is 600 characters or more (our limit, stricter than Claude Code's 1,536 cut). Print ✔ or ✘ per skill and exit 1 if any failed. Test it: change name: fe-codebase to name: frontend-codebase in the fe-guild skill, confirm claude plugin validate plugins/fe-guild --strict still passes, and confirm your script fails.
checks: check_version_bump.py fails on the branch with the unbumped change and passes after 0.4.1.
validate passes with warnings on the PreToolUsee typo, and --strict exits with code 1.
The two risk searches list the hook files and the added allowed-tools line.
Your check_skills.py fails on frontend-codebase while claude plugin validate --strict still passes.

solution.text:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Each skill: its name matches its folder, and description plus when_to_use stays under 600 characters."""
import pathlib
import re
import sys

LIMIT = 600
bad = 0
for skill in sorted(pathlib.Path("plugins").glob("*/skills/*/SKILL.md")):
    head = skill.read_text().split("---")[1]
    field = lambda key: (re.search(rf"^{key}:\s*(.*)$", head, re.M) or [None, ""])[1].strip().strip('"')
    folder, name = skill.parent.name, field("name")
    size = len(field("description")) + len(field("when_to_use"))
    problems = [f"name is {name!r} but the folder is {folder!r}"] if name != folder else []
    problems += [f"description and when_to_use are {size} characters (limit {LIMIT})"] if size >= LIMIT else []
    bad += bool(problems)
    print(f"{'✘' if problems else '✔'} {skill.parent}{': ' + '; '.join(problems) if problems else ''}")
sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)

Why does the workflow install one pinned version of Claude Code instead of the newest one?

check.q: A pull request adds a guard hook under the event name PreToolUsee. CI runs claude plugin validate without --strict. What happens on people's machines after it merges?

options.text: Claude Code refuses to start until the typo is fixed
options.why: Claude Code keeps working with a slightly wrong plugin. That is exactly why the mistake is silent.

options.text: The hook runs before every tool call, because the matcher still matches
options.why: The matcher belongs to the event. An unknown event never fires, so the matcher is never tested.

options.text: Validation passed with a warning, and the hook is ignored on every machine, so the guard never runs
options.why: validate warns that the entry is ignored at runtime. Only --strict turns that warning into a red check.

check.q: Why does the risk job flag a pull request that adds allowed-tools: Bash to a skill's frontmatter?

options.text: Because while that skill is active, Bash runs without a permission prompt on every machine that has the plugin
options.why: It changes what runs without asking, which is a security decision, not a wording change.

options.text: Because allowed-tools is not a valid frontmatter field
options.why: It is a documented field. It is flagged because of what it allows, not because it is wrong.

options.text: Because a skill with allowed-tools fails claude plugin validate --strict
options.why: It validates fine. Validity and risk are different questions.

check.q: A pull request gets the high-risk label. What does that change about how it merges?

options.text: It now needs a second approval from Security
options.why: The repository asks for exactly one approval, always. The label adds information, not an approver.

options.text: Nothing about the rules: the one reviewer is told to run the plugin on their own machine before approving
options.why: The label and the comment tell the reviewer which files run as code, so they test them instead of reading them as text.

options.text: It is blocked until the hook is removed
options.why: Hooks are allowed; rhino-core has two. The label makes sure someone ran them first.

p: plugin-ci.yml in RhinoHealth/claude-plugins runs on every pull request and push to main, and other repositories that hold plugins (rnd-kb-tooling for kb, fcp-local-lab for fcp-lab) call the same workflow. The validate job installs a pinned Claude Code, runs claude plugin validate --strict on both catalogs and every plugin, then scripts/check_skills.py (name matches folder, description plus when_to_use under 600 characters, an owner in catalog.yaml, 3 to 10 eval cases, a warning on capitalised MUST, NEVER or CRITICAL) and scripts/check_version_bump.py. plugin-ci / validate is required in the ruleset.

A secrets job runs gitleaks over the pull request's commits, and a risk job labels changes to hooks, bin/, scripts/, monitors/, .mcp.json or allowed-tools as high-risk with one comment. rhino-core's two hooks, guard_write.py before a write and lint_after_edit.py after an edit, are stdlib Python. The evals job runs claude plugin eval on changed plugins with pinned models. The rollout adds the plugin and MCP keys to the one managed settings policy, pilots on three people for two days, then everyone; agent images seed the stable plugins with CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR.

tickets.why: validate --strict, check_skills.py and the version bump check, as a required, pinned job.
gitleaks and the high-risk label with one comment for the reviewer.
The eval gate that runs after these checks.
The managed settings rollout with the MCP allow-list.

words.plain: The validate flag that turns every warning into an error, so CI fails on problems Claude Code would ignore.
A script that fails when a plugin's files changed but its version in plugin.json did not go up.
A pull request label for changes that run code or skip prompts on every machine; it informs the one reviewer.
A skill frontmatter field that lets the listed tools run without a permission prompt while the skill is active.
A CI check the repository's ruleset makes mandatory: GitHub refuses the merge until it passes.

review.q: Name the three things plugin CI catches before any eval runs, and say for each what would happen on machines without it.
review.a: A manifest or hook problem (--strict): the plugin loads with parts silently ignored. A missing version bump: nobody receives the change. A change that runs code or skips prompts (the risk label): the reviewer reads code as text and approves it untested.

review.q: A teammate wants the newest Claude Code in CI, "so we always validate against the latest rules". What do you answer?
review.a: A new version can add warnings, and with --strict every open pull request turns red at once for reasons unrelated to it. Pin the version and let Renovate raise it in its own pull request, where a new warning is fixed once.

remember: Claude Code forgives plugin mistakes at runtime, so plugin CI must refuse them before merge: validate --strict, a version that goes up with every change, and a label on anything that runs code.
